vocab.articleQuote: paying social-media creators to disseminate short clips of online celebrities
vocab.inContext: Polymarket disseminated the clips — it pushed them out across huge numbers of social-media accounts so that as many people as possible would see them.
vocab.meaning: To disseminate something is to spread it widely, especially information or ideas, so that it reaches a large audience.
examples: The principal used the morning announcements to disseminate the new bell schedule to every classroom at once.
One person posted the rumor, and within an hour group chats had disseminated it across the whole grade.

vocab.articleQuote: create the appearance of a groundswell of authentic interest in a product or brand
vocab.inContext: Here a groundswell means a fast-rising wave of public interest — the kind of genuine excitement Polymarket was faking so its product would look wildly popular.
vocab.meaning: A groundswell is a sudden, strong build-up of public feeling, opinion, or support that seems to rise up on its own from ordinary people.
examples: A groundswell of student support saved the after-school art club from being cut.
One viral clip created such a groundswell of demand that the sneakers sold out in a day.

vocab.articleQuote: The campaign bolstered the perception that Polymarket lets users make fast and easy money
vocab.inContext: The fake videos bolstered a belief — they propped up and strengthened the impression that the site was an easy way to win money.
vocab.meaning: To bolster something is to support or strengthen it, making it stronger, steadier, or more convincing.
examples: She bolstered her essay's argument by adding two quotes from the textbook.
A quick pep talk from the coach bolstered the team's confidence before the final match.

concepts.name: Prediction market
concepts.articleQuote: Commodities law, which governs prediction markets, also bars deceptive and misleading practices.
concepts.meaning:
A prediction market is a place where people bet real money on whether some future event will happen — who wins an election, whether a rocket launches on time, when an album drops. Here is the clever part: because everyone is risking their own money on what they truly expect, the price of a bet turns into a crowd's best guess at the odds. Think of it like a thermometer for likelihood. A contract that trades near 70 cents is the crowd saying 'about a 70% chance'; if the event starts to look doubtful, sellers pile in and the price slides toward 30 cents.

You can watch this live. The market linked below tracks who people think will win the 2028 U.S. presidential election — the number beside each candidate is essentially the crowd's current estimate of their chances, and it slides up and down as news breaks and new bets come in.

Do these markets beat polls? Often they do about as well or better. Prices update the instant news breaks, and because bettors are risking real money, they are pushed to wager on what they think will happen, not what they hope will. In the 2024 U.S. presidential race, betting markets leaned toward the eventual winner more confidently than many poll averages did, which earned them a lot of attention. But it is debated, not settled: a market can be "thin" (very few bettors), can be swung by a single huge bet, and often just echoes the very polls it is supposedly beating — and, as this article shows, it can be deliberately manipulated. So treat a market price as one useful, fast, money-weighted signal of the odds — not a crystal ball.

concepts.name: Astroturfing
concepts.articleQuote: repost the videos from sockpuppet accounts that hid their Polymarket affiliation
concepts.meaning: Picture a lawn. 'Grassroots' support is real grass — it springs up on its own because ordinary people genuinely care about something. Astroturfing is the fake version, named after AstroTurf, the artificial grass in stadiums: a company or group secretly manufactures what looks like that spontaneous, grassroots enthusiasm. They pay or coordinate lots of people — usually hiding who is behind it — so an idea, product, or campaign looks far more popular and trusted than it really is. For example, imagine a new energy drink quietly paying dozens of students to post 'I'm obsessed with this' without admitting they were paid: overnight it looks like the whole school discovered it on its own, when really one company staged the entire wave. The tell-tale signs are the ones this article describes — accounts that hide who they work for, near-identical talking points, and a suspiciously sudden surge of praise — and learning to notice them is a core media-literacy skill.

concepts.name: Insider trading
concepts.articleQuote: a webpage devoted to integrity that reads: “Insider trading is strictly prohibited.”
concepts.meaning: Imagine two people bidding on a sealed box, guessing what is inside — except one of them has already peeked. That contest is a sham, because one side knows the answer everyone else is only guessing at. Insider trading is that same unfairness with money: buying, selling, or betting using important information that isn't public yet. For example, if an employee learns her company will be bought next week — news that will send its stock price jumping — and quietly buys shares before the public finds out, she is pocketing an almost sure profit from a secret everyone else will only learn later. That is why it is considered unfair, and in the stock market it is illegal: a fair market depends on everyone working from the same public information, and insider trading breaks that by letting a few people cash in on what they alone know.

concepts.name: Disclosure (a “material connection”)
concepts.articleQuote: Many of the creators didn't disclose they were paid by Polymarket until we reached out.
concepts.meaning: When someone recommends a product, one hidden fact changes everything: were they paid to say it? A 'material connection' is any tie — usually money — between an advertiser and the person promoting something that could change how much you should trust the pitch. U.S. rules (enforced by the FTC) say that tie has to be revealed, for instance with '#ad' or 'sponsored,' so you can weigh the recommendation knowing money changed hands. For example, a YouTuber who gushes 'these are the best headphones I've ever owned' while hiding that the brand paid her thousands is borrowing your trust dishonestly — the exact same words with a clear '#ad' would let you judge them for what they are. Hiding the payment is deceptive precisely because an endorsement feels far more convincing when you believe it is unpaid and genuine — which is the very trust the creators in this story were taking without earning.

quiz.question: The investigation found that about 10% of the videos implied the creators had won their bets — nearly $900,000 in all. What did the Journal find would have actually happened to anyone who placed those same bets?
options: They would have won even more than the videos showed
They would have roughly broken even
They would have lost more than $166,000
The bets were impossible to trace
quiz.explanation: The Journal traced how each bet would really have resolved and found the creators — and anyone copying them — would have lost more than $166,000, not won.

quiz.question: Which sentence uses the word 'bolster' correctly?
options: The heavy rain bolstered the game, so it was canceled.
Extra evidence bolstered her theory, making it much harder to argue against.
He bolstered the vase off the shelf and it shattered.
The team bolstered the field before the match started.
quiz.explanation: To bolster is to support or strengthen something; extra evidence strengthening a theory fits that meaning.

quiz.question: Polymarket paid thousands of users to repost its videos from accounts that hid the connection, to fake a wave of genuine public enthusiasm. What is this tactic called?
options: Insider trading
Astroturfing
Disclosure
A prediction market
quiz.explanation: Secretly manufacturing fake grassroots support is astroturfing — a play on 'grassroots,' since AstroTurf is fake grass.

quiz.question: The clipping strategy aimed to 'create the appearance of a groundswell of authentic interest.' A groundswell is best described as:
options: A sudden, powerful rise of public feeling or support
A legal complaint filed with regulators
A small, private group of wealthy investors
A hidden fee charged on every bet
quiz.explanation: A groundswell is a rapid, strong surge of public opinion or support that appears to come from ordinary people.

quiz.question: U.S. advertising law generally requires a paid promoter to reveal that they were paid. Why does that disclosure matter?
options: So the company can be charged extra taxes on the ad
So the audience knows money changed hands and can judge the endorsement accordingly
So the video is allowed to be posted in more countries
So the creator is guaranteed to earn more money
quiz.explanation: Disclosing a paid ('material') connection lets viewers weigh a promotion honestly, since a hidden payment makes an endorsement seem more trustworthy than it really is.
